extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates or graduate students studying algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's Foundations of Algebraic Geometry)
extracted.subtask_short: scheme theory: Noetherian and structure sheaf
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts definitions, theorems, and helpful exercises about Noetherian rings/spaces, the correspondence V↔I between geometry and algebra, the construction/properties of the structure sheaf OSpec A, and the basic definition of schemes. Intended as foundational guidance for doing and checking arguments in scheme theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposition of closed subsets in Noetherian spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: In a Noetherian topological space every closed subset can be written as a finite union of irreducible closed subsets; one may assume none of these irreducible closed subsets contain any others. Such a decomposition is unique up to ordering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives the uniqueness proof: if Z = Z1 ∪···∪ Zr = Z'1 ∪···∪ Z's with none containing another, then each Z'i is contained in some Zj and vice versa, forcing equality of the lists. When using this fact, discard redundant components (those contained in others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Connected components vs irreducible components
rubrics_metrics.description: Every connected component of a topological space X is the union of irreducible components of X. Any subset of X that is simultaneously open and closed must be the union of some connected components of X. In a Noetherian topological space the union of any subset of the connected components is open and closed; in particular connected components of Noetherian spaces are open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are useful structural facts about topology on schemes and are presented as exercises (3.6.Q). Note the parenthetical warning: connected components need not be open in general topological spaces, so the Noetherian hypothesis is essential for the stronger conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian ring (ascending chain condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A ring is Noetherian if every ascending sequence of ideals eventually stabilizes: I1 ⊂ I2 ⊂ ··· with stabilization Ir = Ir+1 = ··· (the ascending chain condition on ideals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the primary definition used throughout; many subsequent properties and equivalences build on this notion (see Important Exercise 3.6.S for an equivalent formulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent characterization: finitely generated ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: A ring A is Noetherian if and only if every ideal of A is finitely generated (Important Exercise 3.6.S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equivalence is central to many arguments (e.g., Hilbert Basis Theorem). The text marks this as an 'IMPORTANT EXERCISE'—prove both directions when using the Noetherian property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic examples and permanence properties of Noetherian rings
rubrics_metrics.description: Fields and Z are Noetherian. Noetherianness is preserved by quotients: if A is Noetherian and I an ideal then A/I is Noetherian. Noetherianness is preserved by localization: if A is Noetherian and S a multiplicative set then S^{-1}A is Noetherian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are 'quick facts' presented as straightforward exercises; they are the typical closure properties used when building Noetherian rings from known ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert Basis Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is Noetherian, then A[x] is Noetherian (Theorem 3.6.17).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text provides a proof strategy: given an ideal I ⊂ A[x], inductively choose generators f1, f2, … by minimal degree; consider initial coefficients ai and use Noetherianness of A to reach a contradiction unless the process terminates. This theorem yields that polynomial rings over fields or Z are Noetherian, and hence many finitely generated algebras are Noetherian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spec A Noetherian ↔ A Noetherian (non-equivalence warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is Noetherian then Spec A is a Noetherian topological space (Exercise 3.6.T). However, if Spec A is Noetherian, A need not be Noetherian (counterexamples provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the forward implication freely; beware using the converse without checking algebraic hypotheses. The text gives an explicit example where Spec A is a single point (hence Noetherian) but A is not Noetherian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian module (ascending chain condition on submodules)
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-module M is Noetherian if it satisfies the ascending chain condition for submodules (i.e., every ascending chain of submodules stabilizes). Equivalently, A is Noetherian iff A is a Noetherian A-module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concept parallels Noetherian rings; many module-theoretic arguments follow the same patterns as ideal arguments. Exercises (3.6.V–3.6.Y) relate Noetherian modules to finite generation and exact sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of Noetherian modules in exact sequences and sums
rubrics_metrics.description: If 0 → M' → M → M'' → 0 is exact, then M is Noetherian iff M' and M'' are Noetherian (Exercise 3.6.W). Finite direct sums A⊕⋯⊕A of Noetherian modules are Noetherian (Exercise 3.6.X). If A is Noetherian and M is finitely generated, then M is Noetherian (Exercise 3.6.Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are standard module-theoretic closure properties; the suggested proofs use ascending chains and images/preimages in exact sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical guidance about Noetherian hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Most mathematicians will rarely need to worry about non-Noetherian rings, but pathologies can appear (e.g., fibered products or normalizations of Noetherian rings may be non-Noetherian). One should know when Noetherian hypotheses enter arguments, but not be overly worried about them in routine work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is informal advice (Section 3.6.21) emphasizing awareness: either prove results without Noetherian hypotheses when needed, or accept working in the generality of schemes and recognize the role of the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of I(S): ideal of functions vanishing on a subset S ⊂ Spec A
rubrics_metrics.description: Given S ⊂ Spec A, I(S) := {f ∈ A : f vanishes on S} is an ideal of A (the set of functions vanishing on S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic observations: I(S) is an ideal; I(S) is radical (if f^n ∈ I(S) then f ∈ I(S)); I(·) is inclusion-reversing: S1 ⊂ S2 ⇒ I(S2) ⊂ I(S1). Exercises 3.7.A–3.7.D illustrate these facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: V and I nearly inverse; correspondence between closed sets and radical ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: The maps V(·) and I(·) give an inclusion-reversing bijection between closed subsets of Spec A and radical ideals of A: closed subsets ↔ radical ideals (Theorem 3.7.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the identities V(I(S)) = closure(S) and I(V(J)) = √J. These are fundamental to the 'dictionary' between algebra and geometry; Exercise 3.7.C/D and Theorem 3.7.1 make this precise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreducible closed subsets ↔ prime ideals; generic points
rubrics_metrics.description: V(·) gives a bijection between irreducible closed subsets of Spec A and prime ideals of A; consequently each irreducible closed subset has precisely one generic point (Exercise 3.7.F/G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This translates geometric irreducibility to the algebraic notion of primality. The minimal primes correspond to irreducible components; in Noetherian rings there are finitely many minimal primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal primes and irreducible components
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimal prime ideals of A are in bijection with irreducible components of Spec A; in particular Spec A is irreducible iff A has exactly one minimal prime (Exercise 3.7.G). Every Noetherian ring has finitely many minimal prime ideals (Proposition 3.6.15 and related exercises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to analyze connectedness and decomposition of Spec A; in affine n-space the irreducible components of V(f) correspond to distinct irreducible factors of f (Exercise 3.7.H).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the structure sheaf OSpec A on distinguished opens
rubrics_metrics.description: For an affine ring A and distinguished open D(f) ⊂ Spec A, define OSpec A(D(f)) to be the localization of A at the multiplicative set of all functions that do not vanish outside V(f) (equivalently Af). This depends only on D(f) and not on the choice of f. By Theorem 4.1.2 these data define a sheaf on the distinguished base and hence a sheaf on Spec A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concretely one identifies Γ(D(f), OSpec A) ≅ A_f; OSpec A(∅) = {0}. The construction gives restriction maps by further localization when D(f') ⊂ D(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction maps and compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If D(f') ⊂ D(f) then there is a natural restriction map res_{D(f),D(f')} : OSpec A(D(f)) → OSpec A(D(f')) given by the canonical localization maps; these compose in the obvious way and make the distinguished opens into a presheaf which satisfies the sheaf axioms (hence a sheaf).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When checking sheaf properties, it suffices to verify base identity and base gluability on the distinguished base (Exercises 4.1.B–4.1.C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheaf axioms for OSpec A: base identity and base gluability (exact sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove OSpec A is a sheaf on the distinguished base the key is to establish base identity and base gluability for a cover Spec A = ⋃ D(fi). This is encoded in the exact 'equalizer' sequence 0 → A → ∏ A_{fi} → ∏ A_{fi fj} (Equation (4.1.3.1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text provides explicit arguments: base identity via quasicompactness and clearing denominators; base gluability via a partition-of-unity-style argument producing a global section r from local data ai/gi using a finite subcover and relations r = ∑ r_i b_i / h_i. For infinite covers reduce to finite subcovers using quasicompactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete identification of stalks and sections determined by germs
rubrics_metrics.description: For the structure sheaf, the stalk at a point [p] is the localization A_p; more generally, sections of the structure sheaf are determined by their germs. The canonical isomorphism between the stalk OSpec A_{[p]} and A_p is described (Exercise 4.1.E,F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justifies thinking of elements of A as 'functions' on Spec A whose value at p lies in the residue field κ(p). Use stalk-localization identifications when checking local properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheaf associated to an A-module M (quasi-coherent example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an A-module M, define a presheaf by M(D(f)) := localization of M at the multiplicative set of functions nonvanishing outside V(f); with analogous restriction maps this defines a sheaf on the distinguished base and hence an OSpec A-module (Exercise/Definition 4.1.D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important consequences: the equalizer exactness (4.1.6.1) holds for M, M can be embedded into the product of localizations Mf1×···×Mfr, and stalks satisfy M_{[p]} ≅ M_p. These are the basic facts underlying quasicoherent sheaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support of an element and module
rubrics_metrics.description: For m ∈ M define Supp m := { [p] ∈ Spec A : m_p ≠ 0 } and Supp M := { [p] ∈ Spec A : M_p ≠ 0 }. These supports are closed subsets of Spec A (Definition 4.1.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support is compatible with the sheaf-theoretic notion of support; these notions reappear in later discussions (e.g., associated points in §6.6). Use localization to test vanishing at points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of affine scheme and scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: An affine scheme is a ringed space isomorphic to (Spec A, OSpec A) for some ring A. A scheme is a ringed space such that every point has an open neighborhood U for which (U, OX|_U) is an affine scheme. The Zariski topology is the underlying topology on a scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The structure sheaf and topological space together define the affine scheme; many properties can be recovered from global sections (see next item). Isomorphisms of schemes are isomorphisms of ringed spaces (homeomorphism of spaces plus compatible isomorphism of sheaves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovering the ring from an affine scheme (global sections)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is an affine scheme X ≅ Spec A then Γ(X, OX) = A. More generally Γ(D(f), OSpec A) ≅ A_f. One can recover A from the affine scheme as its ring of global sections; there is a natural isomorphism Spec Γ(X,O_X) ≅ X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the concrete reassurance that affine schemes encode exactly the ring A. The text suggests Exercise 4.3.A to make bijections between ring isomorphisms and scheme isomorphisms explicit (with care to avoid circular reasoning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of affine opens and disjoint unions
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a scheme and U an open subset, then (U, OX|_U) is a scheme; affine opens form a basis for the Zariski topology (4.3.D). The disjoint union of finitely many affine schemes is affine; an infinite disjoint union of nonempty affine schemes need not be affine (4.3.E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are routine but important topological/structural facts about schemes—use quasicompactness to detect non-affineness of infinite disjoint unions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed subschemes: non-uniqueness of scheme structure on vanishing sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Closed subsets of a scheme can be endowed with multiple natural scheme structures; for example, in Spec k[x], the ideals (x) and (x^2) have the same vanishing set but different scheme structures (4.3.5 remark).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This warns that the set-theoretic closed subset does not determine the scheme structure; when working scheme-theoretically, track the ideal (and nilpotents) not just the underlying topological set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally ringed spaces: stalks, maximal ideals, and residue fields
rubrics_metrics.description: A ringed space is locally ringed if its stalks are local rings. For a scheme X the stalk O_{X,p} is a local ring with maximal ideal m_{X,p} and residue field κ(p) = O_{X,p}/m_{X,p}. Functions on an open U have values at p lying in κ(p); vanishing at p means having value 0 in κ(p) (4.3.6–4.3.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational interpretation of 'value of a function at a point' in scheme theory. Many proofs and definitions rely on evaluating sections at stalks or working modulo maximal ideals.
